source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (PNAS, full text via Europe PMC PMC12232635)
finding: Main numbers re-checked in the full text. GPT Base raised practice scores but lowered later unaided exam scores. GPT Tutor (teacher solutions and hints in the prompt) removed the harm but gave no gain on the exam.
numbers: About 50 classes, nearly 1,000 students, grades 9-11, four 90-minute sessions, randomised by class to control, GPT Base, GPT Tutor. Practice: +0.137 (GPT Base, +48%) and +127% (GPT Tutor). Exam: GPT Base -0.054 of 1 (-17%, significant); GPT Tutor -0.004 (not different from control). GPT Base correct only 51% of the time on 57 practice problems, asked 10 times each: 42% logical errors, 8% arithmetic errors.
quote: Specifically, GPT Base often provides incorrect answers due to hallucinations
limits: Randomised by class, not by student. Only one subject (maths) and one exam right after the sessions. The GPT Tutor prompt needed teacher-written solutions per problem, so it is labour heavy. The 51% figure is for the question 'What is the answer?', not for hint-giving.
agent_relevance: A helper that answers is a crutch. Lessons or hints must withhold the answer and be checked against a verified solution. Harm shows up on the unaided test, so test the agent without the lesson as well.

source: PNAS correction to Bastani et al. (2025) (Europe PMC PMC12403119, Crossref)
finding: The 20 Aug 2025 correction only fixes one author's affiliation (Osbert Bastani, University of Pennsylvania) after a production error. No result or number was changed.
numbers: Correction published 20 Aug 2025, PNAS 122(34) e2518204122. Zero changes to the 48%, 127%, -17% or 51% figures.
limits: The separate SSRN design critique (4898213) was still not read, so design objections (class-level assignment, one-shot exam) are untested here.
agent_relevance: The Bastani numbers can be quoted. Gap 2 about the correction is closed; the size of the harm for other models and tasks is still open.

source: HintMR (2026) hint-assisted reasoning for small models (Table 1, full PDF)
finding: Hints from a large model help every small solver tested, and the gain tracks headroom. The weakest solvers on the hardest set gain most in points; a solver that is already strong gains least. Untrained small-model hints can hurt.
numbers: LLM-hint accuracy vs no hint. NuminaMath (N=75): Qwen2.5-Math-7B 46.67 to 78.67; R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 44.00 to 69.33; R1-Distill-Llama-8B 42.67 to 68.00; Phi-4-mini 21.33 to 33.33. MATH-500 (N=74): Qwen2.5-Math-7B 75.68 to 85.14 (+9.5); R1-Qwen-7B 64.86 to 82.43 (+17.6); Llama-8B 52.70 to 71.62; Phi-4-mini 56.76 to 77.03. AIME-2024 (N=29): R1-Qwen-7B 20.69 to 68.97; Llama-8B 0.00 to 44.83. AIME-2025 (N=15): Llama-8B 6.67 to 6.67 (no gain).
limits: Small test sets (15 to 75 items), so one item is 1.3 to 6.7 points. All solvers are 4B to 8B; no solver above 8B, so 'three sizes' is not met. Hints were produced with the solution or final answer known (GPT-5.2 for AIME-2025), so this is oracle-informed scaffolding.
agent_relevance: Hints help a weak solver more than a strong one. On MATH-500 the strongest solver (Qwen2.5-Math-7B, 75.68) gained +9.5, the weaker ones +17 to +20. Expertise reversal not seen for good hints, only for bad ones.

source: HintMR (2026) untrained small-model hints (Table 1 and section 5.3)
finding: Hints from a non-fine-tuned 7B hinter are unstable and often below no-hint. The same hinter after fine-tuning is safe.
numbers: Non-fine-tuned small-model hints vs no hint. MATH-500: Qwen2.5-Math-7B 75.68 to 54.05 (-21.6); Llama-8B 52.70 to 52.70. NuminaMath: Qwen2.5-Math-7B 46.67 to 36.00; Llama-8B 42.67 to 26.67. AIME-2024: Qwen2.5-Math-7B 13.79 to 10.34; Phi-4-mini 6.90 to 0.00. Fine-tuned small hinter on MATH-500: R1-Qwen-7B 64.86 to 85.14; the authors say fine-tuned hints never degrade performance.
quote: unaligned hints can actively hinder structured reasoning
limits: Hints from a model of the same size that was not trained to hint. N of 74 items: 21.6 points is 16 items. Fine-tuned hinter trained on oracle hint traces.
agent_relevance: Hint quality is a gate. A hint-giver that has not been checked can lower a good solver by 20 points. Keep a rule: use a hint only when the hinter was validated for the task.

finding: Stepwise hints beat self-consistency at about one-sixth of the tokens for R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Self-consistency gave no gain on the hardest sets.
limits: Token count is for the solver; hint-generation tokens by the helper are not in the table and wall-clock time was 2 to 3 times higher than no-hint. One solver model. Closes the earlier 'not re-opened' status of the 64.86 and 82.43 figures.
agent_relevance: At equal or lower solver tokens, a good scaffold beats plain resampling. Tests the equal-compute question for hints, not for lessons.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank with MaTTS: memory-aware test-time scaling (section 4.2, Figure 4)
finding: At the same number of trajectories (k=5), scaling with stored lessons beats scaling without memory by a wide margin. This is the first equal-compute baseline for lessons found. Best-of-N without memory was nearly flat.
numbers: WebArena Shopping subset, Gemini-2.5-flash. No-memory scaling fluctuates 39.0 to 42.2 (parallel) and 37.4 to 40.6 (sequential) over k=1 to 5. With ReasoningBank: parallel 49.7 (k=1) to 55.1 (k=5); sequential 49.7 to 54.5. Memory but no aggregation (vanilla TTS): 52.4 parallel, 51.9 sequential at k=5.
quote: Increasing k generally improves success rate
limits: One benchmark subset (187 Shopping tasks), one backbone for the scaling curve. Final answer is picked by an LLM judge, so best-of-N without memory is only as good as that judge. Authors designed MaTTS, so they have a stake.
agent_relevance: Lessons plus the same retries beat retries alone: 55.1 vs about 42 at k=5. Keep a retry-only arm in our test.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank (Table 1, failure ablation)
finding: Memory beats no memory on all backbones read; lessons from failures help ReasoningBank but not the older memory methods. Agent steps fall too.
numbers: WebArena overall (684 tasks), Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 40.5% (9.7 steps), Synapse 42.1, AWM 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8 (8.3 steps), +MaTTS (k=5) 51.8 (7.9 steps). Gemini-2.5-pro no memory 46.7; Claude-3.7-sonnet no memory 41.7. Shopping subset with failures: ReasoningBank 46.5 (success only) to 49.7 (with failures); Synapse 40.6 to 41.7; AWM limited or reduced.
limits: LLM-as-judge decides success or failure, so the lesson signal is noisy. The baseline is no memory, not a retry loop.
agent_relevance: Write lessons from failures too, not only from wins. Expect a few points per backbone, not a jump.

finding: A memory that keeps and rewrites solutions across questions lifts frontier models a lot on some tasks, and little on others. Part of the gain comes from the empty-memory instructions alone.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet: AIME 2024 23.3 baseline, 36.7 with the empty-memory prompt (DC-), 50.0 with cumulative memory. AIME 2025 6.7, 23.3, 36.7. GPQA-Diamond 59.6 to 68.7 (DC-RS). GPT-4o: Game of 24 10 to 19 (empty-memory) to 99 (retrieval and synthesis); AIME 2024 20.0 to 36.7 to 40.0. GPT-4o MMLU-Pro Eng 53.2 to 51.2 (DC-RS, lower).
limits: AIME is 30 items per year (one item is 3.3 points). Game of 24 gain is one reusable Python snippet. Memory is built on the test stream, using model solutions without labels.
agent_relevance: Always run an empty-memory control with the same instructions. On AIME 2024 about half of Sonnet's gain (13.4 of 26.7 points) came from the scaffold text, not stored lessons.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: majority voting and full-history baselines (sections 4 and 5)
finding: Lessons beat a repeated-sampling baseline, and curated lessons beat just appending the full history. Appending uncurated history can hurt.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024: baseline 23.3, majority vote of 3 samples 23.33, DC- 36.7, MV on DC- 33.3, DC-Cu 50.0. AIME 2025: 6.7, 6.7, 23.3, 23.3, 36.7. Full-history appending: Sonnet 26.7 vs DC 50.0 (AIME 2024); GPT-4o 20.0 baseline fell to 6.7 under full-history, 40.0 under DC-RS.
limits: Vote size is 3 and not matched in tokens to the memory run; 30 questions. This is partial support for equal-compute, not a clean match. Author-designed method.
agent_relevance: Raw history is not a lesson. A lesson needs filtering and rewriting. Closes part of Gap 3: a voting baseline exists (no gain), but token-matched retry is still untested.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: smaller models and ordering (Table 3, section 4.6)
finding: Smaller models cannot use stored lessons well. The authors say related questions early may help (a curriculum), but did not test the order.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Haiku AIME 2024: 10.0 baseline, 36.7 DC-Cu, 30.0 DC-RS; AIME 2025 0.0 to 13.3 to 10.0. GPT-4o-mini AIME 2024: 16.7 baseline, 20.0 empty-memory, 13.3 DC-Cu and DC-RS (both below baseline); GPQA 34.3 to 32.3.
quote: tasks arranged to present related questions early may accelerate and improve the model's test-time learning
limits: Ordering claim is a suggestion in the text, not a measured result. Small N.
agent_relevance: Lessons need a capable model to retrieve and apply them (gain tracks solver strength, the opposite of HintMR's external hints). Gap 10 stays open: no ordered-vs-random test for in-context lessons.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), AppWorld Table 1
finding: An evolving playbook built from execution feedback beats fixed demonstrations, a prompt optimiser, and Dynamic Cheatsheet, and still works without ground-truth labels.
numbers: AppWorld, DeepSeek-V3.1 base, average of normal and challenge splits. ReAct 42.4; +ICL 46.0 (+3.6); +GEPA 46.4 (+4.0); +Dynamic Cheatsheet 51.9 (+9.5); +ACE with labels 59.4 (+17.0); +ACE without labels 57.2 (+14.8); ACE online 59.5 (+17.1). ACE cut adaptation latency and rollouts by 75.1% vs GEPA.
limits: Single backbone; the table text is garbled in places and the row-to-number match uses the paper's own summary. Authors built ACE.
agent_relevance: Own-outcome feedback is enough to get most of the gain (14.8 of 17.0). Fits the rule: lessons from verified outcomes.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) ACE: feedback quality limits
finding: Without a reliable outside signal (labels or execution outcomes), both ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet can get worse.
numbers: The paper states that without reliable feedback both ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet may degrade. On financial tasks ACE beat ICL, MIPROv2 and GEPA by 10.9% on average only when ground-truth answers were given.
quote: in the absence of reliable feedback signals ... both ACE and other adaptive methods such as Dynamic Cheatsheet may degrade
limits: No numbers for the degraded case are given in the text read. Finance table not parsed.
agent_relevance: Confirms K20: write lessons only on verified outcomes.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (Table 1)
finding: Machine-induced workflows from the agent's own successes beat 14 human-written workflows on WebArena. A second source on lesson origin.
numbers: WebArena, gpt-4-0613: BrowserGym baseline 23.5%; SteP (14 human expert workflows) 33.0%; AWM online 35.5% (7.6% relative above SteP, 12.0 points above BrowserGym, 51.1% relative). About 2 fewer steps per task than BrowserGym.
limits: Different agent harnesses (SteP vs BrowserGym), so the human-vs-induced comparison is not controlled. GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Self-induced lessons from own successes can match hand-written ones. Together with ExpeL (d14) this answers Gap 4 only in part: own and hand-written are comparable, but no study here compares own-failure lessons against stronger-model lessons with the same writer.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL ablation of lesson source (section 5.6, Table 3, re-opened)
finding: Learned insights beat hand-crafted ones; a stronger insight writer beats a weaker one; adding reflections to insight extraction hurts. The writer (gpt-4) is also the stronger model, so 'stronger writer' is confounded with 'learned from experience'.
numbers: HotpotQA success rate (%), actor gpt-3.5-turbo: ReAct about 28.0; hand-crafted insights about 32.0; insights with reflections 29.0; gpt-3.5 as insight writer 32.0; ExpeL (gpt-4 writer) 39.0 +/-1.7. The PDF table is garbled; row order is inferred from the text claims.
limits: Row-to-number mapping inferred. HotpotQA only for this ablation. Insights from the existing few-shot examples only gave no gain over ReAct: experience is needed.
agent_relevance: Writer strength matters (+7 over gpt-3.5 writer). No lessons without real experience.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Progressive-Hint Prompting (Tables 2 and 3)
finding: Feeding a model its own earlier answers as hints helps more when the model is stronger, and when the first-pass answers are better. Weak models can lose.
numbers: PHP-Complex CoT average gain on text-davinci-002 +1.86 (AQuA -0.4); on text-davinci-003 gains larger (GSM8K +4.6 vs +3.6 for 002; AQuA +1.2). PHP-Standard on text-davinci-002 averages 49.43 vs 49.91 base (-0.48). Base answer quality: PHP-Standard GSM8K 16.0 with Standard base, 50.2 with CoT base, 60.3 with Complex CoT base.
limits: Self-hints (earlier answers), not teacher hints. Old models (2023). Authors say stronger models need fewer interactions.
agent_relevance: Self-generated hints behave like stored lessons: they need a capable base. External hints (d03) behave the other way. Rule: split solver strength from hint source.

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne, Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning (Scientific Reports, full text)
finding: Harvard physics crossover RCT, details re-opened. The advantage is on an immediate post-test of a single lesson. No delayed retest and no second course.
numbers: Fall 2023, Physical Sciences 2, enrolled N=233, two groups, two weekly lessons (surface tension, fluid flow). Median post-score 4.5 (AI, N=142) vs 3.5 (in-class, N=174); pre-test median 2.75. Linear regression effect size 0.63; quantile regression (ceiling-corrected) 0.73 to 1.3; p < 1e-8. Median time on task 49 minutes vs 60 (assumed) in class.
limits: One university, one course, one semester, two topics. Tutor was built with research-based pedagogy (step-by-step, answer-withholding) and the authors built it. Time on task for class assumed. Authors list retention and spacing as future work.
agent_relevance: Supports answer-withholding scaffolds; gives no evidence on persistence. Gap 9 stays open: no replication in other courses was found and no delayed test.
